newsitem.title: UK: North Sea oil hitches dull non-OPEC supply growth.
newsitem.headline: North Sea oil hitches dull non-OPEC supply growth.

text.p: Oil flows this year from producers outside OPEC are failing to match expectations for a second year running, leaving more room for the cartel's crude and helping keep the heat under world oil prices, analysts said on Friday.

Market pundits are cutting their forecasts for 1997 non-OPEC supply growth by around 300,000 barrels per day (bpd), mainly because of a disappointing performance in the North Sea where several new fields have failed to start pumping on time.

"It's been a case in the North Sea of a lot of new technology and really aggressive timescales which have not been realistic enough," said Steve Scullion of Edinburgh-based consultants Wood Mackenzie.

Six months ago oil market analysts were looking to a wave of new oilfield starts in British and Norwegian waters to lead a surge in supplies from nations outside the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries.
Technical setbacks and bad weather held back growth in 1996.

But delayed first oil from half a dozen fields in Norwegian and British waters, further weather delays amid niggling production problems on the giant Brent and Forties systems could alone trim North Sea supply growth forecasts by 150,000 bpd.
And any further problems bringing on stream the 15 or so fields due in the second half of the year could knock a further 50,000 bpd off estimates.

Early this month, the International Energy Agency (IEA), which monitors oil market trends for Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) members, said non-OPEC supply should reach 45.3 million bpd, still 1.8 million bpd up on 1996 but 300,000 bpd below its December estimate.

The Washington-based Petroleum Finance Co (PFC) said slower supply growth had been a major factor in keeping world oil prices nearly $3 a barrel higher on average this year than in four years from 1991-1995
"It's a mixed picture but the market is looking more balanced than earlier this year because of the downward (non-OPEC) revisions," said Mohammad Abduljabbar, PFC's senior economist.
Similar opinions can be found among policy makers in Saudi Arabia, OPEC kingpin and the world's biggest oil exporter.

Last week a well-placed Gulf source told Reuters Saudi expectations for demand on OPEC crude oil in 1997 had been revised up by about 700,000 bpd since the end of last year due to higher than expected demand and non-OPEC's problems.

Oil major British Petroleum Plc has suffered the most serious setback so far, unable to start producing at its pioneering 120,000 bpd Foinaven field in deep Atlantic Ocean waters west of the Shetland Islands.

The troubled project, which is now running well over a year behind schedule, was pushed back by three or four months in May when the company said it would have to remove equipment from the seabed for inspection and possible repair.
Norway's Saga Petroleum ASA said on Thursday it had postponed the start up of the North Sea Tordis East oilfield to the fourth quarter of the year.
But there are still some bright spots, said analysts, pointing to Latin America and Asia where Brazil, Argentina and China continue to perform well.
Even the U.S. could record its first increase in domestic oil production for the first time in 12 years, according to the Independent Producers Association of America (IPAA).

"After the North Sea, the next biggest growth area is Brazil and everything seems to be going fine down there. I don't think the non-OPEC supply story has fallen apart just yet," said a senior oil market analyst.
